title: How to Become a Thought Leader: Agents, Stages & Getting Seen
guestBio: Jacquelyn Fletcher Johnson is the author of 14 books, a keynote speaker, executive coach, and former editor-in-chief and national conference designer. Named one of J.P. Morgan Chase's 100 Women to KNOW in America and featured in The Washington Post, Chicago Tribune, and Psychology Today, she is the founder of The Gateway Project and host of the Ideas Love Community podcast — on a mission to get brilliant women seen, heard, and amplified.
excerpt: If you've ever felt the nudge to write a book, take the stage, or share your ideas with the world — and then talked yourself out of it — this episode is your permission slip. Jacquelyn Fletcher Johnson breaks down exactly how women with something important to say get found by agents, booked on stages, and amplified far beyond their current circle.
metaDescription: Author & speaker coach Jacquelyn Fletcher Johnson on how to become a thought leader, find a literary agent, and get on stages. Ep 81 of The Manage Her®.
keyTakeaways: Visibility isn't vanity — it's distribution for an idea that could change someone's life, and keeping it to yourself is the real selfish act.
A rejected pitch has absolutely no bearing on your worth; your idea can be critiqued, but your value cannot be touched.
Before you share something, run it through three lenses: Is it mine to share? What is the gift in sharing it? Will sharing it harm me?
The nudge toward your idea never fully goes away — treat it as sacred, steward it with intention, and trust that it chose you for a reason.
Literary agents make a decision in roughly 30 seconds, so open your query letter with a curiosity hook, sound unmistakably like yourself, and show the agent you actually know their work.
Build a meaningful track record of paid speaking engagements before approaching a speaking bureau — bureaus amplify momentum, they don't create it.
Amplifying another woman's visibility doesn't diminish your own; the ecosystem expands when women open doors for each other.

quiz.title: What Kind of Thought Leader Are You?
quiz.description: You have ideas worth sharing — but how you carry them into the world is uniquely yours. Answer these six questions honestly (there are no wrong answers) to discover your Thought Leadership archetype and what your next bold move looks like.

A.name: The Visionary Architect
A.description: You think in systems and frameworks, and your ideas tend to arrive as fully realized structures before you've figured out how to talk about them. You're most energized when you can see how all the pieces connect — and most frustrated when others can't see what seems so obvious to you. Your superpower is creating maps for territory other people haven't named yet. This episode will help you find the right rooms to put those maps in front of people who have the power to amplify them.

B.name: The Story Keeper
B.description: Your most powerful currency is lived experience — you turn personal truth into universal wisdom in a way that makes people feel profoundly less alone. You've been told your whole life that you should write a book or give a talk, and you've deflected every single compliment with practiced humility. The world doesn't need you to be more polished; it needs you to be more willing. This episode gives you the practical tools and the emotional permission to stop keeping your story to yourself.

C.name: The Quiet Catalyst
C.description: You are the person in every room who changes the temperature simply by being present — you ask the question no one else thought to ask, and you leave people thinking differently than when they arrived. But you tend to work your magic behind the scenes, crediting the room rather than yourself. You haven't fully claimed the stage because you're not sure you want it — or you're not sure you deserve it. This episode will help you get honest about whether invisibility is wisdom or fear wearing wisdom's clothes.

D.name: The Ready Launcher
D.description: You have done the inner work, you know your message, and if you're being honest, you've been waiting for someone to tell you it's time. You are not stuck on worthiness — you're stuck on mechanics. How do you actually find an agent? What goes in a query letter? When do you need a speaking bureau? This episode is essentially a masterclass built specifically for where you are right now, and Jacquelyn Fletcher Johnson is the guide you've been looking for.

options.text: I want to understand the logic of the critique — is the framework actually flawed, or is this a perspective issue?

questions.question: When you think about your community of peers and collaborators, you'd describe it as:

options.text: Smart and capable, but mostly thinking within the same lane I'm in.
Deep but small — I have a few people who really know me.

questions.question: If you had to describe the relationship between your idea and your identity, you'd say:

options.text: My idea is the clearest expression of how I see the world — it's deeply me, even if it isn't all of me.
My story and my idea are the same thing. Sharing one means sharing both.
I'm still untangling where I end and the idea begins.
I've learned to separate them — my idea has value independent of how I feel about myself on any given day.

content:
You have an idea. Maybe it has been living in you for years — showing up in the margins of your journal, surfacing in conversations when a colleague says, "You should write a book about that." And maybe you have done what so many brilliant women do: nodded politely and then talked yourself right out of it. Not yet. Not qualified enough. Not ready.

This episode of The Manage Her® is a direct response to that voice. Host Aimee Rickabus sits down with Jacquelyn Fletcher Johnson — author of 14 books, executive coach, conference architect, and the woman known in certain circles as the "speaker whisperer" — for a conversation that is equal parts practical roadmap and permission-giving wake-up call.

The Gateway Gathering: Part TED, Part Shark Tank

Jacquelyn's flagship event, The Gateway Gathering & Pitch Fest, was born over a single cup of coffee with TED's Monique Ruff-Bell. What started as a journal sketch became a conference designed specifically for the woman who has something urgent to say and doesn't yet know how to say it in a room that can actually do something with it. Think curated pitches, expert feedback, and the kind of community that doesn't just applaud you — it opens doors for you. The next gathering is October 6–8, 2026 (virtual), and Manage Her® listeners can attend using Aimee's affiliate link with promo code AIMEE.

Your Idea Is Not Your Value

One of the most disarming moments in this conversation comes early. Jacquelyn introduces the concept of trail angels — the gatekeepers, the agents, the conference curators who can feel impossibly powerful from the outside. Her reframe is simple and radical: they are just people. And crucially, when they pass on your idea, they are passing on an idea. Not on you. Your idea can be critiqued. Your value cannot. If you have ever let a single rejection collapse your entire sense of worthiness, this episode will do something for your nervous system that no amount of positive self-talk has managed to do.

Three Lenses Before You Share

Jacquelyn offers a grounding framework for deciding what is yours to put into the world. Before you share a story, a concept, or a chapter of your experience, she asks you to hold it up to three questions: Is it mine to share? What is the gift in sharing it? Will sharing it harm me? This isn't gatekeeping — it's stewardship. It's the difference between oversharing in a way that leaves you exposed and purposeful vulnerability that creates genuine connection and impact.

The Practical Playbook: Agents, Query Letters, and Speaking Bureaus

If you have ever wanted someone to walk you through the actual mechanics of the publishing and speaking world without the insider gatekeeping, this is your episode. Jacquelyn demystifies the literary agent search with refreshing honesty: agents decide in roughly 30 seconds whether your query letter earns more of their attention. Your opening line needs a curiosity hook. Your voice needs to sound unmistakably like you. And you need to demonstrate that you have actually read this agent's work — not just blasted a form letter to 200 inboxes. She also addresses the "no AI" signal that is increasingly expected, and yes, she means it.

On the speaking side, Jacquelyn draws a clear line that most aspiring keynote speakers miss: speaking bureaus amplify existing momentum — they don't create it. Before you approach a bureau, you need a track record of paid engagements, a clear niche, and a reel that makes a booker's job easy. She breaks down exactly what that looks like and when the investment in bureau representation actually makes sense.

Why Accomplished Women Stay Invisible

This is the part of the conversation that might hit closest to home. Jacquelyn names the three reasons she sees accomplished, brilliant women staying small: fear, perfectionism, and loneliness. Not lack of talent. Not lack of ideas. Loneliness — the kind that comes from doing meaningful work in isolation without a community that reflects your ambition back at you. The antidote isn't more hustle. It's the right ecosystem, the right room, and the radical act of letting another woman see all of you — credentials and doubts alike.

The Lava Bracelet

Jacquelyn closes with a story about a lava bracelet she wore onto a stage in front of 2,000 people. It was a physical reminder, a talisman she carried with her: This is not as scary as cancer. It's the kind of reframe that sounds almost too simple until you realize how often we manufacture mountains out of visibility. The stage, the query letter, the pitch — none of it is as scary as the alternative of never trying. That bracelet is a whole philosophy. And it belongs in your pocket every time fear tells you to sit down.

Whether you're a founder with a framework the world needs, an executive who has been quietly told she should write that book, or a woman who has simply carried a nudge for longer than she wants to admit — this episode is for you. The nudge, Jacquelyn says, never fully goes away. Honor it. Steward it. And let this conversation be the first step toward getting it seen.
